title: Self-Hosted LLM: Hardware, Cost, and Setup Guide for 2026
summary: A self hosted llm keeps your sensitive information within your own network. You can evaluate hardware requirements and select models for secure use.
body_markdown:
## The technical stack for local model execution


Precise alignment of GPU memory and software architecture is required for local execution to ensure that sensitive data never leaves your organizational perimeter.


While cloud-based models like[Claude Fable 5.1](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview) offer high-reasoning capabilities for agentic work, replicating that performance on-premise demands a rigorous calculation of hardware overhead.


### Hardware requirements: VRAM is the primary bottleneck


Maximum model size is determined by Video Random Access Memory (VRAM). It's the hard ceiling for local intelligence.


To run a flagship 70B parameter model at 16-bit (Full) precision, your system requires[140 GB](https://rdp.in/gpu-mart/knowledge-base/how-much-vram-does-a-70b-405b-llm-need-for-inference/) of VRAM. This necessitates a multi-GPU cluster like an NVIDIA H100 node rather than a single workstation.


Requirement drops to 70 GB when you use 8-bit (INT8) quantization. This allows the model to fit within the memory of a single A100 or H100 card, so you can bypass the coherence of distributed computing.


For edge deployments or budget-constrained environments, 4-bit (INT4) quantization brings the requirement down to 35 GB, so a single high-memory professional card can now host the model locally.


This allows the model to run on larger-memory enterprise cards like the L40S, which democratizes access to high-capacity AI.


### VRAM requirements and multi-GPU setups


Deploying a 70B model at 4-bit quantization requires 35-43 GB of VRAM, a figure that exceeds standard consumer hardware but fits high-end consumer or professional cards.


A single RTX 4090 offers only 24GB, which is insufficient for this workload and will result in an immediate out-of-memory error, forcing users to either distribute the model across multiple GPUs or reduce its precision, so the hardware is effectively useless for this specific task without significant compromises.


To bridge this gap, users must utilize a multi-GPU setup by pooling the memory of two consumer cards via the system bus.


Alternatively, a single enterprise-grade L40S card provides 48GB of VRAM, allowing the model to fit comfortably on one piece of silicon, so long as the weights are compressed to a 4-bit or 8-bit format.


### Interconnect speed and the consumer hardware bottleneck


Consumer hardware faces a physical limitation when scaling beyond a single card.


While two RTX 4090s provide 48GB of total VRAM, they lack the high-speed NVLink interconnect found on enterprise cards, forcing data to travel over the significantly slower PCIe bus, which creates a severe performance bottleneck during inference.


This hardware constraint creates a massive communication bottleneck during inference. Without a dedicated high-speed bridge, the latency penalty of moving data between consumer GPUs can negate the benefits of a larger model, making enterprise silicon mandatory for high-performance private clusters.


### Choosing between Ollama, vLLM, and LocalAI


Hardware efficiency and the ease of integration with existing internal services are dictated by your choice of inference engine.


vLLM is a high-throughput library that uses PagedAttention to manage memory. It allows for 24x higher throughput than basic implementations, effectively enabling real-time responsiveness for demanding applications, so users experience near-instantaneous feedback during complex interactions.


Hundreds of concurrent users can query the same hardware, drastically lowering the cost-per-request for service providers, thereby making large-scale AI deployment economically viable, so the financial barrier to entry for high-traffic applications is significantly reduced.


Ollama is a streamlined tool that bundles model weights and configurations into a single "Modelfile."


This simplifies the deployment of models like Mistral Large 4 for your teams without dedicated MLOps engineers. LocalAI is a drop-in replacement for OpenAI’s API that supports multiple backends. You can redirect legacy applications to local infrastructure without rewriting code.


### Model quantization: Balancing speed and intelligence


Memory is saved by reducing the bit-precision of model weights, but quantization introduces a trade-off between resource efficiency and reasoning accuracy.


While high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification are best served by smaller, faster models like[Claude Haiku 5.5](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview) , local deployments often use quantization to squeeze larger models into available VRAM.


Precision VRAM Required (70B Model) Impact on Deployment


16-bit (Full) 140 GB Requires multi-GPU NVLink clusters; no loss in reasoning.


8-bit (INT8) 70 GB Fits on a single high-end enterprise GPU; negligible accuracy drop.


4-bit (INT4) 35-43 GB Runs on high-end consumer hardware; slight degradation in complex logic.


*Prices and plan limits checked against[docs.claude.com](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview) and[openai.com](https://openai.com/chatgpt/pricing) and[gemini.google](https://gemini.google/subscriptions) on October 12, 2026.*


A 4x reduction in hardware costs is possible when moving from 16-bit to 4-bit, yet the resulting "perplexity" increase may lead to hallucinations in regulated legal or medical summaries, forcing developers to weigh financial savings against the risk of critical inaccuracy, meaning that cost-cutting measures could compromise the reliability of sensitive outputs.


The financial savings come at the expense of output reliability. Selecting the right quantization level keeps your system within budget without sacrificing the reliability required for compliance-heavy workflows.
